title: A Podcast on Minimalism
description: Four recordings about minimalism: a podcast introduction, two friends decluttering, an interview with an author and a disagreement between flatmates.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A podcast introduction
parts.intro: You will hear Hana introducing the first episode of her podcast about minimalism.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Hello and welcome to Simple Living. I'm Hana, and in this first episode I want to answer a question I get asked all the time: what actually is minimalism?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Many people picture an empty white room with one chair and a single plant. That image is misleading. Minimalism isn't about owning as little as possible. It's about owning only what adds value to your life, and letting go of the rest.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: For me, the turning point came three years ago, when I moved flats. I discovered that I owned eleven coats, although I only wore two of them. I'd been paying to store and clean things I never used.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: I started with a simple rule: if I haven't used something for a year, it goes. I expected to feel sad. Instead, I felt lighter, and I saved time every morning because choosing what to wear became so easy.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: My friends thought I'd gone a bit strange at first. One of them even asked whether I was planning to run away to the mountains. But after a few months, several of them were quietly asking me for advice.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Of course, minimalism isn't magic. It won't make you happy by itself, and it's easy to turn it into another competition, with people boasting about how little they own. That rather misses the point.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: What it can do is give you space, in your home, your budget and your attention. In this series, I'll be talking to people who've tried it, and I promise not to ask anyone to throw away their books.

parts.title: Part 2 · Two friends
parts.intro: You will hear Ben visiting his friend Linh, who has been decluttering her flat.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Linh, your flat looks enormous! Did you move the furniture?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: No, I got rid of it. Well, half of it. I've been following a decluttering challenge for the past month.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: A challenge? What does that involve?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: On day one you throw away one thing, on day two, two things, and so on. By the end of the month, you've let go of nearly five hundred items.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Five hundred? Where did it all go?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Some to charity shops, some to friends, and I sold a few things online. I made about ninety pounds from an old camera.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Ninety? I'd have thought it was worth more. Anyway, wasn't it hard to let go of stuff?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: The hardest part was sentimental things. Cards, old school books, my grandmother's teapot. In the end, I kept the teapot and took photos of the rest.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Clever. I couldn't do it. My place is a disaster, and I always say I'll tidy up at the weekend.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Start small. Do one drawer, not the whole house. Honestly, the first drawer is the most difficult.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Hmm. Would you help me this Saturday?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Only if you promise not to keep every cable you own.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Deal. Though I might need them.

parts.title: Part 3 · An interview with an author
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Minh, interviewing Clara, the author of a book about living with less.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: My guest is Clara, author of a book called Enough. Clara, what made you write it?

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Frustration, mostly. I worked in advertising for ten years, and my job was to persuade people they needed things they didn't. One day, I looked around my own house and realised I'd fallen for my own tricks.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: That's a striking confession. Did you quit?

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Not straight away. I stayed another year, partly because of the mortgage. But I changed how I lived, and eventually I left to write.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Some critics say minimalism is a luxury. You need money to throw things away and buy better ones.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: There's some truth in that, and I take the criticism seriously. If you can't afford a new coat, you shouldn't throw away the old one. For me, minimalism means being thoughtful rather than wasteful. It can mean repairing, borrowing, and buying second-hand.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: So it's more about attitude than possessions.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Exactly. A person with a tiny flat full of objects they love can be more of a minimalist than someone with a huge, empty house who is constantly buying the next gadget.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: I imagine that attitude affects how you shop, too.

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Hugely. I wait a month before buying anything expensive. About half the time, I discover that I've simply forgotten about it.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: And what would you say to someone who feels overwhelmed by their belongings?

script.speaker: Clara
script.text: Don't judge yourself. Ask one question about each item: does this make my life better today? If the answer is no, you have your answer.

parts.title: Part 4 · Flatmates
parts.intro: You will hear two flatmates, Emma and Nam, talking about their living room.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: Nam, I've been thinking about the living room. It's full of your stuff, and I'd like to clear some of it.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: My stuff? The shelf of games is mine, I admit, but the sofa and the lamp are both yours.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: True, but I'm thinking about the boxes by the window. You've had them for six months.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: They're for my hobby. I'm going to build a model railway one day.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: One day. You've said that since March. Honestly, I think we'd both be calmer in a tidier space. I read that clutter increases stress.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: I'm not convinced. I'm actually more relaxed when I'm surrounded by things I like. A bare room feels cold, like a hospital waiting room.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: I'm not suggesting a bare room. I'd just like a clear table and a floor I can walk across.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: That's reasonable, I suppose. What if I give myself a deadline? If I haven't started the railway by the end of next month, I'll sell the boxes.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: Deal. And I'll move my plants to the balcony to make room, so it's fair on both of us.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: All right. But the games stay.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: The games can stay.
